n: After the Flood, all people share one language. This story explains how the many languages and nations of chapter 10 came about.

f.g: Literally “one lip and the same words.”

n: Migrating people settle on a plain in Shinar, the region of Babylon in southern Mesopotamia.

f.g: Or “eastward”; in Genesis, moving east often hints at moving away from God.

n: Lacking stone, they bake mud bricks and use tar as mortar—real building methods of ancient Mesopotamia. The narrator gently contrasts their human-made materials with God’s creation.

f.g: An old expression meaning “Come on!” or “Let’s go!”
Bitumen or tar.
Thoroughly.

n: They plan a city and a towering structure to reach heaven and make a name for themselves. Their aim is human glory and security without God—exactly the opposite of God’s command to fill the earth.

f.g: Likely a ziggurat, a stepped temple-tower common in Mesopotamia.

f.w: let us make us a name

n: With gentle irony, the narrator says the Lord had to “come down” to see the tower that was supposed to reach heaven. Their greatest effort is tiny to God.

f.g: A picture of God investigating before judging (compare Genesis 18:21).

n: God observes that a united humanity bent on pride will stop at nothing. Unity is good, but unity in rebellion only multiplies evil.

f.w: nothing will be restrained from them
f.g: Nothing will be impossible or held back for them.

n: God speaks again in the plural, “let us,” and confuses their language. Their own “let us” plans are answered by God’s “let us.”

f.g: To mix up or confuse.

n: God scatters them, and construction stops. What they feared—being scattered—happens anyway. The Book of Mormon tells of the Jaredites, who came from the tower and were led by God to the Americas.
The place is called Babel, which sounds like the Hebrew word for “confuse.” Babylon claimed its name meant “gate of God,” but Genesis turns the name into “confusion.”

f.g: Wordplay with Hebrew balal, “to confuse.” Babylonians understood Bab-ili as “gate of god.”

n: The story narrows from all nations to one family line, Shem’s, which leads to Abram. God’s plan to bless all nations will come through one family.

f.w: These are the generations of Shem

n: Shem lives five hundred more years. By the Bible’s numbers he would have lived into Abram’s lifetime.

f.g: Lifespans begin decreasing noticeably after the Flood.

n: Arphaxad fathers Salah. Notice how the ages at which men become fathers are now much younger than before the Flood.
Arphaxad lives 403 more years.

f.g: Years Arphaxad lived after Salah’s birth.

n: Salah fathers Eber, the ancestor of the Hebrews.
Salah lives 403 more years.

f.g: Years Salah lived after Eber’s birth.

n: Eber fathers Peleg, in whose days the earth was divided.
Eber lives 430 more years.

f.g: Eber’s total life of 464 years is the longest after Shem’s in this list.

n: Peleg fathers Reu. From Peleg on, lifespans drop sharply.

f.g: Means perhaps “friend.”

n: Peleg lives 209 more years—his total of 239 is about half that of his father.

f.g: Years Peleg lived after Reu’s birth.

n: Reu fathers Serug.

f.g: Also the name of a town near Haran in northern Mesopotamia.

n: Reu lives 207 more years.

f.g: Years Reu lived after Serug’s birth.

n: Serug fathers Nahor, Abram’s grandfather.

f.g: Abram will also have a brother named Nahor (verse 26).

n: Serug lives two hundred more years.

f.g: Years Serug lived after Nahor’s birth.

n: Nahor fathers Terah, Abram’s father.
Nahor lives 119 more years.

f.g: Nahor’s total of 148 years is the shortest in this list.

n: Terah becomes father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. With Abram, the story of God’s covenant people truly begins.

f.g: Means “exalted father”; later renamed Abraham (17:5).

n: Terah’s family record is introduced, including Lot, Abram’s nephew, who will play an important role in coming chapters.
Haran dies in Ur, his hometown. The book of Abraham says Ur was full of idolatry, and that a famine struck the land.

f.g: Usually identified with Ur in southern Iraq, though some propose a northern location.

n: Abram marries Sarai, and Nahor marries his niece Milcah. These family ties will matter later, when Isaac and Jacob find wives among Nahor’s descendants.

f.g: Possibly “princess”; later renamed Sarah (17:15).

n: A brief, heartbreaking note: Sarai cannot have children. This sets up the central tension of Abram’s story—how can God’s promise of countless descendants come true?

f.g: Unable to have children.

n: Terah leads the family out of Ur toward Canaan, but they stop and settle in Haran. The book of Abraham clarifies that the Lord called Abraham to leave Ur, and Terah followed.

f.w: they went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldees

f.g: A trading city in northern Mesopotamia (modern Turkey), not the same as Abram’s brother Haran.

n: Terah dies in Haran at 205. The book of Abraham records that Terah returned to his idolatry there.
